title: Skin-contact whites
subtitle: The orange wine revival
objectives: Explain how orange wine is made
Explain Friuli's role in its revival

steps.title: White grapes, red method
steps.body: Orange, or amber, wine is made from white grapes fermented on their skins, like a red, for days, weeks or months. Skins give the wine an amber colour, tannin, texture and flavours of dried fruit, tea, nuts and orange peel. It's an ancient method, preserved in Georgia, with its clay qvevri.

steps.title: Friuli's pioneers
steps.body: In the late 1990s, Friuli producers like Josko Gravner and Stanko Radikon, in Oslavia in the Collio, began making long skin-contact whites, mainly from Ribolla Gialla. Gravner travelled to Georgia and from 2001 fermented in buried qvevri. Their wines inspired a worldwide orange wine movement.

steps.prompt: Which grape is central to Friuli's orange wines?
steps.explanation: Ribolla Gialla's thick skins suit long maceration.

steps.title: Taste and style
steps.body: Orange wines are dry, with tannin and texture unusual for white wine, and flavours of apricot, orange peel, tea, honey and nuts. Many are made with minimal intervention, little or no sulphur, and natural yeasts. They're often served slightly warmer than whites, around 12 to 14 degrees, in larger glasses.

steps.prompt: What do skins give an orange wine?
steps.explanation: Orange wines are dry; skins don't add sugar.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Orange wine ferments white grapes on their skins
Gravner and Radikon in Friuli revived it from the late 1990s
It's dry, tannic and textured, served a little warmer
